title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial-Intelligence Software in Intraoral, Panoramic, and CBCT Imaging: A Pilot Study
content:
Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in dental radiology, but its performance may depend on the imaging modality and analytical model. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based software (Diagnocat) in intraoral, panoramic, and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images against an expert reference standard, accounting for both pathological findings and "no pathology" indications. 

Methods: In this retrospective analysis, 45 anonymized examinations (15 intraoral radiographs, 15 panoramic radiographs, and 15 CBCT) were assessed. The reference standard was set by an expert in radiology with over 30 years of experience. The unit of analysis was a single diagnostic indication, covering both the presence and the absence of pathology. For each modality, a "pathology vs. no pathology" matrix was built and sensitivity, specificity, precision (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), accuracy, and F1-score were calculated; associations were tested with the Pearson χ² test. 

Results: Overall, 990 indications were recorded in the reference standard and 1017 by AI. Intraoral radiographs yielded sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.59, precision 0.72, and F1 0.69; panoramic radiographs 0.66, 0.88, 0.79, and 0.72 (the highest specificity); and CBCT 0.74, 0.86, 0.78, and 0.76 (the highest sensitivity and accuracy, at the cost of more additional indications). All associations were statistically significant (p = 0.038 for intraoral; p < 0.001 for panoramic and CBCT). 

Conclusions: Diagnostic accuracy was clearly modality-dependent. Treating "no pathology" indications as true negatives allowed specificity to be calculated and clinical usefulness to be assessed more realistically. The software may support the interpretation of dental radiographs but should not replace expert assessment.
